Says echarts and zrender sit in the lazy reports chunk that src/routes.js loads with import(), so they do not delay the first screen, and ranks them below the initial-chunk fixes

Measures the main entry's initial JavaScript as the vendors and main chunks, 311,282 bytes of emitted JavaScript (301,412 + 9,870, minified, before compression), in one unit system, and does not present the sum of all chunks as what the first load downloads. It gives no compressed figure as measured: any gzip number is labelled an estimate or replaced by a way to measure it after a build

Finds date-fns installed twice, naming node_modules/date-fns (pulled in by src/utils/format.js) and node_modules/@tidal/daterange-picker/node_modules/date-fns (pulled in by the picker, a CommonJS copy), and proposes aligning the versions so one copy is installed rather than removing date-fns from the app

Gives the lodash fix from the functions format.js actually uses (groupBy, sortBy, round) as per-method imports, lodash-es named imports or native code, and notes from the stats that format.js is the only importer
Does not promise the pre-minification module size as the download saving, and says the saving is confirmed by rebuilding and comparing
Proposes a per-entry budget on the main entry's initial JavaScript, with a threshold in the unit of the tool that enforces it
Does not invent the version of the nested date-fns copy or the picker's required range, which are not in the input, and says how to read them (for example npm ls date-fns)
Keeps the reply lean: the answer first, a short numbered list of fixes, no full module or package table

evals.prompt: PR #318 on our order console failed the bundle-size check; PR.md has the CI output and the author's comment. meta-before.json and meta-after.json are the esbuild metafiles from main and from the PR branch. Should we raise the limit like the author suggests? What actually grew?
assertions: Answers first that raising the total limit is the wrong fix, because the change that slows the first load is in the main entry, not the lazy Analytics route

Attributes the first-load growth to papaparse (19,480 bytes) and file-saver (2,690 bytes) imported statically by src/components/ExportButton.tsx through src/components/Toolbar.tsx, 23,344 bytes added to the main entry's initial JavaScript (159,050 to 182,394)
Attributes the larger growth, 195,230 bytes, to @tidal/heatmap in the Analytics chunk that src/App.tsx loads with import(), and says it does not land in the first load
Recommends loading papaparse and file-saver with a dynamic import when the export button is clicked, and says what to check after (the export still downloads a correct CSV)

Proposes a per-entry budget on the main entry's initial JavaScript (plus, optionally, a separate figure for the Analytics route) and says that budget would have caught this PR's first-load growth while a total-size limit only flagged the lazy growth
Gives no invented compressed sizes: the metafile bytes are minified and uncompressed, and with no built files any gzip figure is labelled an estimate or replaced by a way to measure it
Does not invent load times, Lighthouse scores, user counts or sizes that cannot be computed from the metafiles and PR.md
Keeps the reply short and answer-first, without a table of every chunk and module

Can we just remove it? And what else is making the first load heavy? We'd like the first load under 60 KB gzipped.

Names the way to shrink it (replace the date picker with one built on a smaller date library or a native input, or keep the picker and drop the bundled locales) and what to check (formats, locales and time zones the calendar uses)

Identifies the core-js polyfills from import of core-js/stable in src/main.tsx (58,250 bytes rendered, 21,454 bytes gzipped per the visualizer) in the initial index chunk, and checks them against the browserslist in package.json (Chrome and Edge 111, Firefox 115, Safari 16.4), which have these features natively

Measures the first load as 75,974 bytes gzipped across the index and vendor chunks, from the visualizer's figures, says it is over the 60 KB target and that removing core-js brings it to about 54,500 bytes
Does not present react-dom as something to remove
Does not invent which locales the app needs, the picker's internals, or a moment version beyond what package.json says
Keeps the reply short and answer-first

evals.prompt: Our size bot flagged PR #482 on the support portal (it adds a Reply box under each ticket on the Home page, src/components/CommentBox.jsx) and says main grew a lot. But I diffed the dist folder totals and it's only about +3 KB, so I think the bot is comparing the wrong thing. Before and after webpack stats are in stats/before.json and stats/after.json. Is the bot wrong? And what should we have had set up to catch this properly?
assertions: Answers the question directly up front: the bot is right. The initial `main` chunk grew from 163,000 to 342,900 bytes (+179,900, roughly 176-180 KB), while the all-chunks total grew only 3,400 bytes (347,100 to 350,500), which is the +3 KB the user saw.

Explains why the total barely moved: the editor code (src/components/RichText.jsx 3,900 + @inkwell/editor 141,200 + inkwell-model 31,400 = 176,500 bytes) moved out of the lazy `compose` chunk (184,100 down to 7,600) into the initial `main` chunk. The bytes went from lazy-loaded to first load; little new code was added.

Names the import chain from the `reasons` in after.json: src/routes/Home.jsx -> src/components/CommentBox.jsx -> src/components/RichText.jsx -> @inkwell/editor -> inkwell-model. Notes that src/routes/Compose.jsx is still loaded through import(), so the static import from CommentBox is what drags the editor in.

Recommends a fix that keeps the editor out of the first load: load RichText (or the editor) lazily from CommentBox with dynamic import()/React.lazy, for example when Reply is clicked, which CommentBox.jsx's `open` state already gates. Does not suggest removing the editor, and does not suggest lazy-loading the Compose route, which is already lazy.

Proposes a per-entry budget on the `main` entry's initial JavaScript (for example webpack `performance.maxEntrypointSize` with `hints: 'error'`, or a size-limit style CI check on main), not a budget on total dist size. The threshold it gives passes 163,000 and fails 342,900, and it says explicitly that a total-size budget would have missed this PR.

Is accurate about what the numbers are: the stats `size` values are webpack module sizes, not gzip or brotli bytes. Any compressed figure is either labelled an estimate or comes with a command to measure it from the built files (e.g. `gzip -c dist/main.*.js | wc -c`). It does not present invented compressed numbers as measured.

Invents nothing that isn't in the input: no modules, packages, asset sizes, config files or CI tools described as already present beyond what stats/before.json, stats/after.json and CommentBox.jsx show. For example, it does not claim react-dom or client.js changed.

Stays proportionate to a 'was the bot wrong, how do we guard this' question. It stays on this regression and the budget and does not turn into a full bundle audit (e.g. recommending replacing react or react-dom).

evals.prompt: ops dashboard is really slow to open on the warehouse tablets and someone said the bundle is huge. what can we actually cut without breaking anything? esbuild metafile is build/meta.json, rest of the repo is here
assertions: Answers the question directly with a ranked list of what can come out of the first load. It treats first-load JS as the entry output dist/assets/main-7QX2KD.js (421,400 bytes), leaves the .js.map outputs out of the count, and keeps the lazily loaded dist/assets/Exports-M4PZ1A.js (215,500 bytes) separate.

Ranks glyphset as the biggest first-load cut (198,400 bytesInOutput, about 47% of main) and traces it to src/components/Icon.jsx, where `import * as Icons from 'glyphset'` plus the `Icons[name]` dynamic lookup stops tree-shaking. The fix it gives is explicit imports (or an explicit name-to-component map) of only the icons actually used, plus a way to list the names in use (e.g. grep for `<Icon name=`), since the route sources aren't provided.

Finds tempora bundled twice: v3.1.0 at node_modules/tempora (ESM, 6,900 bytes in main) and v2.9.1 at node_modules/plotline/node_modules/tempora (CJS, 23,800 bytes, not tree-shaken). It gives the chain src/routes/Overview.jsx -> plotline -> plotline's nested tempora, and notes from package-lock.json that plotline 4.2.0 requires tempora ^2.4.0.

Treats the tempora dedupe with care: forcing v3 on plotline (npm overrides/resolutions) is a major-version jump and not a safe removal without checking. The response gives a command to run with network access (e.g. `npm view plotline versions` / `npm view plotline@latest dependencies`) and does not claim that a plotline version supporting tempora 3 exists.

Checks polyfills against .browserslistrc (chrome >= 110, edge >= 110): es.promise, es.array.flat, es.object.from-entries, es.string.replace-all and es.array.at can come out of src/polyfills.js (about 5,950 bytes). es.object.group-by (610 bytes) must stay, because Object.groupBy only shipped in Chrome/Edge 117 and src/utils/groupRows.js uses it. The alternative is to rewrite groupRows and then drop it.

Does not present sheetsmith (214,300 bytes, the biggest single library) as a first-load cut, because it is only reached through the dynamic import of src/routes/Exports.jsx and sits in the lazy Exports chunk. If it mentions sheetsmith, it says it doesn't affect opening the dashboard.

Is accurate that the metafile bytes are minified, uncompressed sizes, not gzip or brotli. Any compressed figure is labelled an estimate or comes with a command to measure it after a build. It does not suggest cutting code needed at runtime (react, react-dom, plotline itself).

Invents nothing that isn't in the input: no package versions, icon names, sizes, files or browser targets beyond what meta.json, package.json, package-lock.json, .browserslistrc and the src files contain. It delivers the cut list instead of stopping to ask clarifying questions first.

evals.prompt: lighthouse keeps dinging our landing page for unused JS. we moved the charts onto a lazy /reports route back in march so i dont get why index-*.js is still ~460k. someone on the team reckons its the echarts locale files? vite build w/ the visualizer plugin, raw data is in stats.json. what can we cut - the german charts have to keep working tho
assertions: Names the import chain that keeps ECharts in the entry chunk assets/index-C7qK2mPa.js despite the lazy route: src/main.tsx -> src/i18n/index.ts -> src/i18n/chartLocales.ts -> echarts/core (imported for registerLocale) -> echarts/lib/core/echarts.js and zrender.

Corrects the team's guess with numbers: the six registered locale files (DE, FR, ES, JA, PT-br, KO) are only about 8.2 KB gzip (8,244 B), while ECharts core + zrender + tslib in the entry total about 67.6 KB gzip (67,604 B), close to half the entry's ~147.4 KB gzip (147,431 B, the sum of per-module gzipLength).

Explains that the ~460k figure is the uncompressed size (the entry's renderedLength sums to 465,132 B), gives first-load JavaScript in compressed terms (~147 KB gzip), and keeps the lazy Reports chunk (assets/Reports-Bf41xQ9e.js, ~40.4 KB gzip / 40,414 B) separate from that figure.

Recommends moving the chartLocales import / registerLocale call off the entry path, into src/pages/Reports.tsx or a module only Reports imports, so echarts/core moves into the lazy chunk. Does not recommend dropping ECharts or undoing the lazy route.

Keeps German working by keeping the DE registration (EN ships with ECharts core via langEN). Says FR, ES, JA, PT-br and KO can be dropped because SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES is only ['en', 'de'], and puts that at about 6.9 KB gzip (6,892 B), a minor saving next to the core move.

Gives the expected outcome as an estimate (entry roughly 80 KB gzip after the move: 147,431 - 67,604 = 79,827 B, with React/react-dom/router at ~73 KB as the remaining floor) and says to confirm it by rebuilding (e.g. `npm run build` / `vite build`) and re-reading stats.json, since per-module gzip sums only approximate the gzip of the whole chunk.
Invents nothing that is not in the input: no module sizes, files, chunk names, ECharts APIs or Lighthouse scores beyond what stats.json and the source files contain.
Answers the actual question directly and at a size that fits a casual ask: leads with what is really heavy and the specific cut(s) to make, rather than a module-by-module audit of the whole bundle.

evals.prompt: I lead frontend platform at Quillmark. Both of our apps in the monorepo (apps/storefront and apps/backoffice, webpack 5) consume our shared component library @quillmark/ui from packages/ui. Storefront only uses Button, PriceTag and Modal, yet its main bundle is enormous. I've committed production stats for both: apps/storefront/stats.json and apps/backoffice/stats.json. I need three things: (1) what @quillmark/ui is costing each app on first load and why, (2) the change to packages/ui that fixes it, plus anything that change could break, and (3) per-entry size budgets we can enforce in CI for both apps so this doesn't creep back.
assertions: Traces the import chain from stats reasons/issuers, e.g. ./src/index.tsx -> ./src/App.tsx -> ./src/pages/Home.tsx -> @quillmark/ui (../../packages/ui/dist/index.js) -> ./Chart -> chart.js/auto -> chart.js/dist/chart.cjs. Names the root cause: packages/ui is compiled to CommonJS (tsconfig "module": "commonjs", only a "main" field, no ESM entry and no "sideEffects"), so the barrel's require() calls pull in every component (the stats show the 'Module is not an ECMAScript module' bailout).

For storefront, gives first-load cost from the CompressionPlugin output: main.8c41d2e7.js is 141,206 B gzip (437,914 B raw). Names the unused weight in it: the DataGrid/DatePicker/Chart wrappers and their dependencies @tanstack/table-core, dayjs, chart.js (with helpers.segment.cjs and @kurkle/color).

Treats webpack module `size` values as pre-minification source bytes, not emitted or gzip bytes. For example, it does not claim the chart.js-related modules' 522,298 B (or the 665,654 B of unused modules) are part of a 437,914-byte asset. Any per-dependency compressed saving is labelled an estimate or comes with a way to measure it after a rebuild. It also notes that backoffice's stats contain no gzip sizes (no CompressionPlugin there).

For backoffice, sees that DataGrid/DatePicker (table-core, dayjs) are really used by Users/Orders in main, but Chart/chart.js is used only by the lazy Analytics route. analytics.e71b4d08.js is just 1,206 B because chart.js already sits in main. Says chart.js will move into the analytics chunk only once main's imports stop going through the CommonJS barrel.

The packages/ui fix ships an ES module build (e.g. ESM output via a "module" field or an "exports" import condition, optionally per-component entry points) and declares side effects while keeping CSS as one (e.g. "sideEffects": ["**/*.css"]), because dist/Button.js does require("./Button.css"). It warns that a blanket "sideEffects": false would silently drop the Button styles.

Budgets are set per entry for each app separately with an explicit unit (gzip vs raw). Notes that webpack's performance.maxEntrypointSize counts uncompressed emitted bytes, that storefront has performance.hints set to false, and that backoffice's 512,000-byte limit did not fire at 451,088 B. Proposes deriving the final numbers from post-fix stats plus headroom, without stating post-fix sizes as measured fact.

Invents nothing that is not in the input: no component names, package versions, file paths, chunk or asset sizes, or webpack/plugin options beyond what the stats and repo files contain. Any tool that would need installing from the network is given as a command, not presented as already run.
Answers all three numbered questions directly, per app, in the order asked.
